score: 91 recommendations and candidates, 0 observed wrong. Rewrites: 72 recommendations, 65 judged and agreeing with the original on the dataset, 7 not judged; none estimated 2% cheaper; 2 ran at least 1.4x faster. Advisor (store_view and unstore_table): 19 candidates, 7 proven and all 7 executed to the same rows (5 recommended), 7 listed as needing proof and 5 refused as changing results, none counted as a saving
metric: KumoSQL's recommended rewrites (the rule pipeline and the proof-gated optimizer) on 103 TPC-DS and 53 DSB statements, and the materialization advisor's store_view and unstore_table candidates on 3 synthetic Dataform projects, judged in a fixed order: correctness first (proof label, then same rows when executed against the original), then the cost estimate, then measured runtime (rewrites only), each reported on its own.
correctness: No wrong result observed. Rewrites, under the stricter comparison (rows as a bag with multiplicity, output column names and types, sort keys including hidden ones, floats to 9 places), on one workload (PostgreSQL scale factor 1, seed 7, rerun 2026-10-03): 65 of 72 recommendations were judged by the row comparator and agreed with the original; 7 rule rewrites were not judged because the original no longer runs on PostgreSQL after the BigQuery round trip the rules need. Proof and dataset agreement are separate facts: 66 of the 72 carry a proof; 6 are unproven (CTE inlining around window functions), of which 5 ran and returned the same rows and 1 (q21) was not judged. Advisor (2026-10-05, offline, DuckDB): each of the 19 candidates, and each project's chosen set, was run for 3 simulated days against the unchanged project, 1,362 reads compared in all (every query and every model, between runs and after the refresh, with a difference counted only when DuckDB with its optimizer off agrees). The 7 proven candidates and the 3 chosen sets returned the same rows. Of the 7 that need proof, 6 returned stale rows between runs (the 7th satisfies its condition in the simulation); all 5 that read a clock, RAND or a UUID returned different rows, so refusing them was right. 0 unproven candidates were recommended or chosen. Agreement on one dataset is evidence, not a proof, and a proof holds only under its stated assumptions
coverage_of: The 72 recommended rewrites from the 156 statements plus the 19 advisor candidates (91 in all), by proof label: 73 carry a proof (66 rewrites, 7 candidates); 13 are not proven (6 rewrites labelled unproven, 7 candidates that need proof); 5 candidates would change results and are refused.
usefulness: Rules: 44 recommendations (27 parenthesis removals, 24 single-use CTE inlinings), all estimated unchanged and none 10% faster or slower; they simplify text, not plans. Optimizer: 28 recommendations, none estimated at least 2% cheaper; two ran faster at an essentially unchanged estimate (TPC-DS q38 1.40x, q87 1.42x), none slower by 10%, so on this draw the estimate predicted no saving and missed two. Advisor: 5 of the 19 candidates are recommended (3 store_view, 2 unstore_table) with a positive estimated daily saving in bytes billed; that saving is an estimate from a synthetic job history, not a measurement, and the advisor's estimate was not compared with a measured saving here. Two proven candidates are not recommended because their refresh costs more than they save, and the largest estimated saving (a join of tables on different schedules) is listed as needing proof, not counted
performance: Median of 5 alternating runs after a warm-up on PostgreSQL 16, TPC-DS and DSB at scale factor 1; geometric-mean speedup 1.001x (rules, 37 judged) and 1.017x (optimizer, 28). The advisor candidates have no runtime measurement
caveats: What "0 wrong" covers: 44 rule and 28 optimizer recommendations on 103 TPC-DS and 53 DSB statements (run 2026-10-03), and 19 advisor candidates on 3 synthetic projects (run 2026-10-05, offline; the rewrite figures were not rerun for this date); it excludes build recommendations, shared-model proposals, cost attribution and change reports. The proof holds under its model (declared keys and NOT NULL hold, floats are never NaN, runtime errors are not modeled, rows tied under ORDER BY or LIMIT may be chosen differently), and the optimizer accepts a rewrite whose estimate is up to 2% higher, so accepted does not mean cheaper. These assumptions are copied into every record the tool writes. This run used the stricter comparator, which appends hidden sort keys and compares output column names and types; floats still compare rounded to 9 decimal places (differences below about 5e-10 are invisible) and agreement on one dataset can never rule out a looser predicate that agrees on the data (WHERE k = 10 against k < 15). The queries were regenerated for this run (TPC-DS templates with the Netezza dialect file, DSB's PostgreSQL templates, dsqgen seed 7, 103 + 53 statements) and are not stored in the repo (TPC licence); the first run's query text was not kept, so this is a fresh draw from the same templates and the two runs' estimates and timings differ (the first run's one estimated saving, DSB query069, did not recur). No held-out split. Estimates are PostgreSQL EXPLAIN costs, a local stand-in for BigQuery dry-run bytes; no real BigQuery run yet. In the first run one optimizer rewrite (TPC-DS q44) compared as different rows because tied rows came back in another order; the comparison now allows ties in any order. Advisor caveats: the projects, job histories and sizes are invented and small (three cases, 60 to 66 reads each), written by the same people who wrote the advisor, so the 19 candidates show that the evidence labels and the gate behave on these shapes, not how often the advisor is right on a real warehouse. A store or un-store changes where a model is computed, not any SQL, so the proof is the advisor's evidence label, and the executed comparison is a check of that label on three days of data in DuckDB with BigQuery SQL transpiled (the transpiler is the same on both sides and not under test). The simulation refreshes every stored model once a day in one run, changes sources only between runs and never reads during a run, which is the model the proven label assumes; a clock is replaced by the simulated date, and RAND and UUID are DuckDB's, seeded and single-threaded. A candidate that is not proven and still returned the same rows (1 of 7) is not evidence that it is safe. No held-out cases: the fixtures were written together with the advisor's tests.
